topInterview.title: INTERVIEW
topInterview.contentTitle: PROBABLY GOING TO REORDER THE PARAGRAPHS BUT THIS IS WHAT I GOT FROM THE INTERVIEW
topInterview.content:
From bands to open mic, from instrument to instrument, Grace Janusz has solidified herself as one of Groton’s most versatile musicians. As the Jazz Band’s baritone saxophone and trumpet player, Grace shows her incredible skill in learning and picking up new styles of music and ways of playing her growing repertoire of available instruments.

What music work did you do before Groton? When did you start playing?Most of my experience in music started just by playing with other kids in school bands. I started playing saxophone in the George Mason elementary school band and jazz band, and then for about three more years at the George Washington middle school symphonic band and jazz band. I mainly played saxophone, but during my Eighth grade year I played the clarinet, and during quarantine I picked up the guitar and ukulele.

What made you choose these instruments?
I really wanted to play the saxophone because I thought it was cool, but after a while I realized I hated the alto saxophone, so much so that I threatened to quit four times before deciding to move to bari sax, mainly because I just discovered that I liked it more, and switching to bari helped me realize what I liked about music.
My other instruments came from wanting to learn an instrument from every section of a band: guitar, bass, and ukulele took up the strings and rhythm sections since percussion wasn’t really for me, and baritone sax took up my woodwinds section, so I decided to start learning trumpet to complete my range of instruments in the brass section.

What’s been your favorite performance so far?
There hasn’t been a specific one that’s my favorite since I’ve been in a lot of performances between the bands I’ve been in before, but one that stands out to me is my Eighth Grade pops concert. We played “Man Eater,” and my friend composed it, so it was really fun playing in front of my school of around 1500 kids.

What’s something you’ve learned from playing music with the bands and other kids at Groton?I think I’ve learned to communicate with “band kids” since there’s a very specific type of person who joins Groton bands, so learning to communicate and collaborate with those types of people is definitely something I’ve learned throughout my time here. I’ve also learned the importance of practice; if you’re good at something, and you don’t practice, there will come a time where you will slowly lose that skill because you decided not to practice. You need to constantly try to grow as a musician in order to truly get better, you can’t just be complacent.

If you could be an instrument/music scale, what would it be?
For instrument I would definitely be an ocarina, and for scale I would be the b flat blues.
What’s your favorite part of music?
I really like when a piece comes together at the end and you can hear everyone play their parts. I actually lost my hearing recently in one of my ears, and that made me realize that I truly enjoyed listening to music. When you can feel the sound fill the room, and everyone does what they should and they have the opportunity to play their part, it just feels and sounds amazing.

What’s your favorite Jazz Band song so far?
I love Groovin’ Hard and Caravan. I played Groovin’ Hard in Eighth Grade District Jazz, and it was actually the first song I ever played on the bari sax. I love it because it’s showed how far I’ve come since now I’ve played the harder version a couple of years later. I also really love Caravan because songs that are super fast are fun to play and learn.

What advice do you have for people that are either coming to learn music at Groton or are currently learning music at Groton?
Make sure to be dedicated, at least in the Jazz Band. A lot of the work there is just practicing, so nobody goes to Jazz Band to just be there and not practice. This also applies to music in general too. Even if you’re bad at something in the beginning, and you think you don’t like it because you’re bad at it or for other reasons, if you truly put in the work and practice, you will get better.
